claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has a single-phase BCC structure.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has high density.
The baseline alloy has insufficient room-temperature compressive ductility and undergoes brittle failure.
The baseline's brittle behavior is caused by a lack of crack-arresting microstructural features.
Adding 1.0–2.0 at.% Si to Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will induce precipitation of a secondary phase.
Solution annealing followed by aging or controlled cooling will promote secondary-phase nucleation in the BCC matrix.
Heat treatment will cause the secondary phase to coalesce into a continuous reticulated network.
The precipitated phase will be a Si-rich intermetallic, potentially B2-type or a Laves phase.
The secondary phase will form a continuous network at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
A reticulated intermetallic network will act as a barrier that pins, deflects, or branches propagating cracks.
Crack deflection by the network will increase fracture toughness and room-temperature compressive ductility.
The proposed improvement depends on the topological continuity of the secondary phase rather than simple solid-solution or particle-dispersion strengthening.
The Si-modified alloy will retain high compressive yield strength through matrix and interface strengthening.
The Si-modified alloy will exhibit a significantly greater fracture strain than the baseline.
Adding Si and forming the secondary phase will marginally increase alloy density.
The beneficial mechanism requires sufficient Si to create a percolating network but not enough to produce gross embrittlement or a continuous brittle shell.
At elevated temperature, the proposed intermetallic network may coarsen or dissolve and thereby change the mechanical behavior.
Rapid quenching after Si addition can suppress formation of the intermetallic network and provide a topology-control condition.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to room-temperature uniaxial compression after vacuum arc melting and controlled cooling or aging.
